note: Interactive lab definitions. Every fact shown in a lab must cite a lesson chunk. Simulator numbers are illustrative and must be labelled as an example.

labs.title: Explore the African catfish in 3D
labs.teaser: Spin, zoom and tap a 3D African catfish to discover its barbels, long fins and air-breathing organ.
labs.instructions: Drag to spin the fish, scroll or pinch to zoom, and tap the glowing points. Switch between fingerling and adult to compare.

model.notes: Eel-like cylindrical body; flattened bony head; four pairs of barbels (nasal, maxillary = longest, inner and outer mandibular); very long dorsal and anal fins reaching nearly to the tail; pectoral fins with a spine as first ray; smooth scaleless skin, marbled dark above and light below. Proportions are approximate and not to scale.

modes.label: Adult
modes.note: An adult African catfish. Proportions are approximate.

modes.label: Fingerling
modes.note: In FAO nursery trials, most fingerlings were about 2–3 g and a minority 8–10 g after four to five weeks (mc-05). Shown larger than life so you can see it.

hotspots.label: Upper-jaw barbels
hotspots.text: The longest and most mobile pair of barbels. Barbels mainly help the fish find food.

hotspots.label: Nasal barbels
hotspots.text: One of the four pairs of barbels, near the nostrils.

hotspots.label: Lower-jaw barbels
hotspots.text: Two pairs of barbels (inner and outer) under the lower jaw.

hotspots.label: Flat, bony head
hotspots.text: The head is flattened and heavily boned.

hotspots.label: Long dorsal fin
hotspots.text: The fin along the back is very long, reaching nearly to the tail, and has only soft rays.

hotspots.label: Long anal fin
hotspots.text: The fin underneath is also very long and soft-rayed.

hotspots.label: Side fin spine
hotspots.text: The first ray of each side (pectoral) fin is a stiff spine.

hotspots.label: Smooth, scaleless skin
hotspots.text: The skin has no scales. It is dark and marbled on the back and sides, lighter underneath.

hotspots.label: Air-breathing organ
hotspots.text: Behind the gills, tree-like structures in air chambers take oxygen straight from the air.

labs.title: Water-source simulator
labs.teaser: Pick a water source, slide through the year and watch whether your pond stays full through the dry months.
labs.instructions: Choose a water source, then drag the slider through the year. Watch the source level against what the pond needs.
labs.exampleNote: Example scenario with made-up numbers for a fictional place. Real water levels depend on your location and season (wa-08).

pondNeed.unit: example units of water per month
pondNeed.note: A pond needs water to fill it and to top it up; it needs more top-ups when it's dry (wa-03).

sources.label: Shared hand-dug well
sources.note: In this example the well drops in the dry months, and other households use it too.

sources.label: Borehole
sources.note: In this example the borehole stays fairly steady. Remember borehole water can differ in quality, so testing matters.

sources.label: Stream below the plot
sources.note: In this example the stream shrinks in the dry months. It is lower than the pond, so water can't flow in by gravity, and it may carry wild fish.

sources.label: Rain only
sources.note: Rain alone is not a reliable way to keep a pond full: dry periods leave it too low.

questions.prompt: In this example, which source keeps up with the pond's needs all year?
questions.explain: Only the borehole stays above the pond's needs every month in this example. Check real sources in the driest months (wa-03).

questions.prompt: For the shared well, in which kind of month is the shortfall biggest?
questions.explain: The gap is biggest in the dry months, which is why the key question is whether water lasts through the driest part of the year (wa-03).

labs.title: Pond builder
labs.teaser: Drag to size a pond with a measuring tape, set the depth and watch the area and volume update live.
labs.instructions: Drag the corner handles or type sizes. Use the depth stick to set depth. The tape shows each side in metres.
labs.math: area = length × width (m²); volume = area × average depth (m³); litres = m³ × 1000. This is a simplified box shape; real ponds have sloping banks.

references.label: FAO suggests a first pond larger than 300 m²
Bigger ponds: at least 0.75 m at the shallow end
Bigger ponds: at least 1–1.2 m at the deepest point

setupTypes.label: Earthen pond
setupTypes.text: Dug into the ground with banks made from the dug-out soil. The most common setup among surveyed farmers.

setupTypes.label: Concrete tank
setupTypes.text: A built tank you will also see in use. These lessons don't yet compare its costs or results.

setupTypes.label: Tarpaulin tank
setupTypes.text: A collapsible tank on a metal frame, often seen in backyards. These lessons don't yet compare its costs or results.

challenges.prompt: Build FAO's worked example: a 20 × 20 m pond.
challenges.explain: 20 × 20 m = 400 m², above the 300 m² FAO suggests for a first pond (so-03).

challenges.prompt: Find the smallest square pond (in 0.5 m steps) that is larger than 300 m².
Fill Emeka's 8 × 6 m backyard completely. How does it compare with 300 m²?
challenges.explain: 8 × 6 m = 48 m², far smaller than the 300 m² FAO suggests for a pond, so a small backyard usually points to other options (so-03, so-06).

labs.title: Spot the warning signs
labs.teaser: Watch animated pond scenes and tap the warning signs of poor water before it's too late.
labs.instructions: Look closely at each pond scene and tap anything that could be a warning sign. Not everything you see is a problem.

scenes.title: A hot afternoon
scenes.context: It has been very hot all day. You visit the pond after the afternoon feed.

elements.label: Fish gulping air at the surface
elements.explain: Fish gathering at the surface to gulp air is a warning sign of poor water. Hot weather can reduce the oxygen available to fish.

elements.label: Uneaten feed floating
elements.explain: Fish eating poorly is a warning sign, and overfeeding can reduce oxygen in the water.

elements.label: A bird resting on the bank
elements.explain: The lesson doesn't list this as a warning sign of poor water.

scenes.title: After a heavy storm
scenes.context: A heavy storm washed soil from the bank into the pond overnight.

elements.label: Very muddy, brown water
elements.explain: Good pond water should not be too muddy.

elements.label: Fish swimming strongly
elements.explain: Strong swimming is not a warning sign. Weak swimming would be.

elements.label: A few leaves on the water
elements.explain: The lesson doesn't list this as a warning sign of poor water.

scenes.title: Feeding time
scenes.context: You throw in feed and watch the fish for a few minutes.

elements.label: Most fish rushing to eat
elements.explain: Fish eating eagerly is a good sign, not a warning.

elements.label: One fish swimming weakly
elements.explain: Fish swimming weakly is a warning sign of poor water.

elements.label: A bad smell from the water
elements.explain: Good pond water should not smell bad.

remedy.text: One remedy in FAO's handbook is replacing part of the pond water with clean water, which depends on having a reliable supply.
